description: Python library and shell utilities to monitor filesystem events.

sources.entry: watchdog - API and shell utilities to monitor file system events.

summary.one_liner: Python API and shell utilities (including the watchmedo command) for monitoring file system events across Linux, macOS, BSD, and Windows.
summary.what_it_does: Provides a Python API where you schedule event handlers on one or more directories (optionally recursive) and receive events such as file creation, modification, deletion, and moves. It includes an optional command-line tool, watchmedo, with subcommands such as log (print events matching glob patterns) and shell-command (run a shell command per event, with variables like watch_src_path). watchmedo can also read tricks.yaml files to run event-handler classes called tricks, which plugin authors write. The library selects a native backend per platform (inotify on Linux, FSEvents or kqueue on macOS, kqueue on BSD, ReadDirectoryChangesW on Windows) and offers a polling observer that compares directory snapshots as a portable fallback. The README also notes the PollingObserver as the recommended choice for CIFS shares and that Vim's backup-and-swap saving prevents modified events from firing.
use_cases: Run a build or test command when source files change
Log file creation, modification, and deletion in a directory tree
Watch a folder for new files and process them
Auto-reload a development server on save
Sync or mirror changes between directories
notable: Cross-platform observers that pick the native OS file-event API, with a polling fallback
watchmedo CLI for logging events or running shell commands without writing code
tricks.yaml plugin system for reusable event handlers configured declaratively
Observer usable as a context manager for clean startup and shutdown
Documents specific quirks such as Vim's swap-file saves and kqueue file-descriptor limits
caveats: kqueue backend needs the file descriptor limit raised (ulimit -n) and scales poorly on large trees
Polling observer is slow and not recommended, though it is needed for CIFS shares
Free-threaded CPython support exists, but a full thread-safety audit has not been completed, particularly for macOS FSEvents
